title: Spread vs Moneyline Betting in Canada: Which Is Better
excerpt: Spread and moneyline bets price the same game two different ways. Here is how Canadian bettors should choose between them, sport by sport and price by price.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Open any Canadian sportsbook and the first decision you face on a given game is structural rather than analytical: do you back a team on the spread or on the moneyline? The two markets describe the same contest with the same information, but they convert your opinion into risk in completely different ways. Understanding the relationship between spread and moneyline betting is one of the few pieces of betting theory that pays for itself immediately, because it stops you from taking the worse of two prices on a view you already hold.

What each market actually asks you

A moneyline bet asks a single question: which team wins? Nothing else matters. A one-goal overtime win and a five-goal rout settle identically. Because outcomes are unequal in likelihood, the price does the work — a strong favourite might pay -220 while the underdog pays +180.

A spread bet, sometimes called the handicap or in hockey the puck line, applies a margin. The favourite must win by more than the number; the underdog can lose by less than it and still cash. Both sides are then priced close to even money, typically around -110 each, so the book's edge comes from the vig rather than from the gap between the two teams.

The key insight is that these are the same opinion expressed at different confidence levels. Backing a -220 favourite on the moneyline says you think they win. Backing that same team at -1.5 says you think they win comfortably. That is a materially stronger claim, and the price rewards you for it.

The sport determines which market is sharper

Where the spread sits relative to the natural distribution of margins matters enormously, and that distribution is different in every sport.

Hockey

NHL games cluster tightly around one- and two-goal margins, and the near-universal 1.5 puck line sits right in the middle of that cluster. That makes puck line bets volatile — a huge share of games finish exactly one goal apart, often into an empty net in the final minute. Taking a favourite at -1.5 in hockey is a genuinely different bet from taking them on the moneyline, not a cosmetic adjustment. Our Canadian sports betting guide covers how those margins break down across a season.

Football

NFL and CFL margins spread far more widely, and certain numbers carry disproportionate weight. In the NFL, three and seven are the most common margins by a clear distance, which is why moving a line from -2.5 to -3.5 changes its value much more than moving it from -5.5 to -6.5. Spread betting in football is a game of key numbers, and bettors who ignore them systematically overpay.

Basketball and baseball

Basketball margins are broadly distributed with no single dominant number, so spreads behave more smoothly and the choice between spread and moneyline is largely a question of how much variance you want. Baseball is the opposite extreme: the run line is fixed at 1.5, a huge share of games are decided by one run, and the moneyline is the primary market for good reason.

Converting between the two

Every moneyline price implies a probability, and comparing that implied probability across markets is how you find the better side of a bet you already want to make. To convert a negative price, divide the odds by the odds plus 100. A -220 favourite implies 220 / 320, or about 68.75 per cent. For a positive price, divide 100 by the odds plus 100: a +180 underdog implies 100 / 280, roughly 35.7 per cent.

Add those together and you get more than 100 per cent. The excess is the book's margin, and it is the reason both markets are negative-expectation bets before you add any handicapping skill. Reducing that margin by shopping for better prices is the most reliable improvement available to any bettor, and it requires no predictive ability at all. If the arithmetic here is new to you, our primer on how sports betting odds work walks through it slowly.

When to prefer each market

A practical framework:

  • Take the moneyline when you like an underdog outright, when the sport has tightly clustered margins, or when you want lower variance on a favourite you are confident in.
  • Take the spread when you believe a favourite is materially stronger than the market thinks, when you want to reduce the cost of backing a heavy favourite, or when the line sits on the wrong side of a key number.
  • Take an underdog on the spread when you think a game will be close but not necessarily won — the points convert a narrow loss into a winning ticket.
  • Avoid laying a big favourite on the moneyline purely because it feels safe. At -400 you are risking four units to win one, and a single upset erases four winners.

That last habit deserves emphasis. Heavy moneyline favourites feel comfortable and are one of the most common ways recreational bettors slowly drain a bankroll. The price already accounts for the mismatch; your comfort is not an edge.

Alternate lines and the middle ground

Most licensed Canadian books now offer alternate spreads, letting you buy points in either direction with the price adjusted accordingly. Used carefully, this is a useful tool for moving a number off a key margin. Used carelessly, it is expensive — books typically charge more for the points than they are strictly worth, particularly around the numbers that matter most. Price out the alternate line against the main one before assuming the safer-looking number is the better bet.

Shop both markets, every time

Because spread and moneyline are priced from the same underlying model, a book that is slightly off on one is often slightly off on the other in the same direction. Holding accounts at several licensed operators lets you take the best available version of whichever bet you want. Ontario bettors can compare licensed options on our Ontario sports betting page, and Albertans will find the equivalent on our Alberta betting guide.

The bottom line

Neither market is inherently better. The spread is better when you have a view on margin; the moneyline is better when you have a view on the winner. The mistake is choosing between them out of habit rather than because the shape of your opinion points to one. Work out what you actually believe about a game — winner, or winner by how much — and let that decide which bet you place. Then check the price at more than one book before you click, because the difference between a good bet and a bad one is frequently just a few cents of vig.
